http-status-codes.assumptionNote: Code names stay in English because they are the official IETF reason phrases; descriptions are localized.
benefits: Look up any status code in seconds with instant search.
Category filters group codes by 1xx informational through 5xx server errors.
Each code explains both what it means and when you will see it.
Fully offline reference — no network needed after the page loads.

c100.desc: The server received the request headers and the client should continue sending the body.
c100.use: Large uploads where the client checks with Expect: 100-continue before sending data.

c101.desc: The server agrees to switch protocols, for example from HTTP to WebSocket.
c101.use: WebSocket handshakes negotiated with an Upgrade header.

c103.desc: The server sends preliminary headers so the client can preload resources early.
c103.use: Servers that want the browser to start fetching CSS or JS before the full response.

c200.desc: The request succeeded and the server returned the requested data.
c200.use: Normal successful GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE responses.

c201.desc: The request succeeded and a new resource was created on the server.
c201.use: POST requests that create a user, order, or record; check the Location header.

c202.desc: The request was accepted for processing but is not complete yet.
c202.use: Background jobs and queues where work finishes asynchronously.

c204.desc: The request succeeded but there is no content to return.
c204.use: DELETE requests and form submissions that need no response body.

c206.desc: The server returned part of the resource as requested with a Range header.
c206.use: Video streaming and resumable downloads that fetch byte ranges.

c301.desc: The resource moved permanently to a new URL; update bookmarks and links.
c301.use: Domain changes and HTTP-to-HTTPS migrations; browsers cache this redirect.

c302.desc: The resource was found but is temporarily at a different URL.
c302.use: Temporary promotions or maintenance pages; not cached like 301.

c303.desc: The response is at another URL and should be fetched with GET.
c303.use: After a form POST, redirecting to a result page to avoid resubmission.

c304.desc: The cached copy is still fresh; the server sent no body.
c304.use: Conditional requests with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since saving bandwidth.

c307.desc: Temporary redirect that preserves the original request method and body.
c307.use: Temporary URL changes for POST or PUT requests that must not become GET.

c308.desc: Permanent redirect that preserves the original request method and body.
c308.use: Permanent URL changes where the method must survive the redirect.

c400.desc: The server could not understand the request because of invalid syntax.
c400.use: Malformed JSON bodies, missing required fields, or bad query parameters.

c401.desc: Authentication is required and missing or invalid.
c401.use: Missing or expired tokens; the response should include WWW-Authenticate.

c402.desc: Reserved for payment-related errors; rarely used in practice.
c402.use: Payment-gated APIs that chose this code for billing failures.

c403.desc: The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it.
c403.use: Logged-in users accessing admin pages or resources they do not own.

c404.desc: The server cannot find the requested resource.
c404.use: Wrong URLs, deleted pages, or mistyped API endpoints.

c405.desc: The HTTP method is not allowed for this resource.
c405.use: Sending POST to an endpoint that only accepts GET.

c408.desc: The server timed out waiting for the client to send the request.
c408.use: Very slow clients or stalled uploads on busy servers.

c409.desc: The request conflicts with the current state of the resource.
c409.use: Creating a user with an email that already exists.

c410.desc: The resource is gone permanently and will not come back.
c410.use: Deleted content where you want search engines to drop the URL.

c413.desc: The request body is larger than the server accepts.
c413.use: Uploads exceeding the server's size limit; check the limit and retry smaller.

c414.desc: The URL is longer than the server is willing to process.
c414.use: GET requests stuffing too much data into query parameters.

c415.desc: The media type of the request body is not supported.
c415.use: Posting XML to a JSON-only API or missing Content-Type.

c422.desc: The request was well-formed but semantically invalid.
c422.use: Validation errors: correct JSON shape but failing business rules.

c425.desc: The server refuses to process a request sent too early.
c425.use: TLS early-data (0-RTT) requests that might be replayed.

c426.desc: The client must switch to a different protocol to continue.
c426.use: Old clients told to upgrade from HTTP/1.0 or plain WebSocket.

c429.desc: The client sent too many requests in a short time.
c429.use: Rate-limited APIs; respect the Retry-After header before retrying.

c431.desc: The request headers are too large for the server.
c431.use: Oversized cookies or too many headers; clear cookies and retry.

c451.desc: The resource is unavailable for legal reasons.
c451.use: Content blocked by court order or government censorship.

c500.desc: The server hit an unexpected condition it does not know how to handle.
c500.use: Unhandled exceptions and crashes in server code; check server logs.

c501.desc: The server does not support the functionality required.
c501.use: Requests for features the server has not implemented.

c502.desc: A gateway or proxy received an invalid response from upstream.
c502.use: Reverse proxies like nginx when the app server crashes or is unreachable.

c503.desc: The server is temporarily unable to handle the request.
c503.use: Overload or maintenance windows; retry later, honoring Retry-After.

c504.desc: A gateway timed out waiting for the upstream server.
c504.use: Slow backend responses behind a proxy or load balancer.

c505.desc: The server does not support the HTTP version used in the request.
c505.use: Very old or very new HTTP versions the server cannot speak.

c507.desc: The server cannot store the representation needed to complete the request.
c507.use: WebDAV uploads when the disk or quota is full.

c511.desc: The client must authenticate to gain network access.
c511.use: Captive portals on public Wi-Fi intercepting the first request.

faqs.a: 1xx means informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, and 5xx server error. The first digit tells you who needs to act: 4xx is usually your bug, 5xx is the server's problem.
faqs.q: What do the code categories mean?

faqs.a: 401 means you are not authenticated — log in or send a valid token. 403 means you are authenticated but not allowed — the server refuses regardless of login.
faqs.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?

faqs.a: Use 301 for permanent moves (browsers and search engines remember it) and 302 or 307 for temporary ones. Use 307/308 instead of 301/302 when the request method and body must survive the redirect.
Yes. 429 tells you to slow down and often includes a Retry-After header with the wait time. Hammering the API anyway can get your key suspended.

faqs.a: 404 means the specific resource was not found. Check the URL for typos, confirm the resource still exists, and for APIs verify the endpoint path and HTTP method.

http-status-codes.formula:
1xx Informational  - request received, keep going
2xx Success        - request received and accepted
3xx Redirection    - follow the Location header
4xx Client error   - fix the request and retry
5xx Server error   - the server failed; retry later

keyFacts: HTTP status codes are three digits sent with every response.
The first digit defines the category: 1xx through 5xx.
Codes are standardized by the IETF in the HTTP specifications.
4xx errors mean the client should change the request.
5xx errors mean the server failed to fulfill a valid request.

http-status-codes.quickAnswer: Every HTTP response carries a three-digit status code: 2xx means success, 3xx means redirect, 4xx means the client made a mistake, and 5xx means the server failed. This reference lists 40 common codes with plain-language meanings so you can diagnose any response in seconds.
http-status-codes.tagline: Look up any HTTP status code — what it means and what to do.
http-status-codes.workedExample:
Your API call returns 429.

Search 429: Too Many Requests — the client sent too many requests in a short time. When you see it: the API is rate-limited; read the Retry-After header and wait before retrying instead of hammering the endpoint.

Compare with 503 Service Unavailable: the server itself is overloaded or in maintenance. Both say wait, but 429 is your quota while 503 is their capacity.
